extracted.intended_audience: aspiring periodical essayists, translators, and literary writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short periodical essays and literary translations (mottos, openings, quotations, and tonal choices) aimed at a broad early-18th-century readership. Includes advice on selecting mottoes, classical allusion, translation fidelity, and anti-patterns in poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose mottos from poets rather than prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When I have finished any of my Speculations, it is my Method to consider which of the ancient Authors have touched upon the Subject... I rather chuse to take out of the Poets than the Prose-writers, as the former generally give a finer Turn to a Thought than the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic lines give a finer turn and are more portable to memory; select short, harmonious lines that encapsulate a thought or similitude relevant to the paper. Use mottoes to provide a memorable opening and to supply authority or a felicitous illustration for the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide at least one memorable line per paper
rubrics_metrics.description: My Reader is therefore sure to meet with at least one good Line in every Paper...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to include a striking or portable sentence/line that will linger in the reader's memory; this can be a poetic motto or a crafted sentence in the body to give the paper extra beauty and recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the motto to support paradoxes or signal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A Motto... is sometimes in a manner necessary when the Writer is engaged in what may appear a Paradox to vulgar Minds, as it shews that he is supported by good Authorities, and is not singular in his Opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place an apt quotation at the head of a piece to preempt reader skepticism when asserting an unconventional claim; the motto signals learned backing and frames the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the body accessible when the motto is learned/obscure
rubrics_metrics.description: I must confess, the Motto is of little Use to an unlearned Reader, for which Reason I consider it only as a Word to the Wise. But... if they cannot relish the Motto, I take care to make Provision for them in the Body of my Paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lead with an obscure or learned quotation, ensure the main text contains clear, plain exposition and entertainment so less erudite readers are not excluded; balance ornament with accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor rhetorical ornaments to your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: I hear the Ladies, whose Approbation I value more than that of the whole Learned World, declare themselves in a more particular manner pleased with my Greek Mottos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rhetorical flourishes (Latin/Greek mottoes, learned allusions) with awareness of what will please the intended readership; different social groups respond to different ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult classical authors for apt similitudes and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: When I have finished any of my Speculations, it is my Method to consider which of the ancient Authors have touched upon the Subject that I treat of. By this means I meet with some celebrated Thought upon it, or a Thought of my own expressed in better Words, or some Similitude for the Illustration of my Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before finalizing a piece, look for classical parallels to enrich phrasing, find concise expressions, or provide illustrative similes; borrow a motto or turn of phrase when it better conveys the thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ playful/obscure signatures or marks to intrigue readers
rubrics_metrics.description: I have made use of these obscure Marks for the same Purpose. They are, perhaps, little Amulets or Charms to preserve the Paper against the Fascination and Malice of evil Eyes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using cryptic initials, marks, or playful sign-offs can create curiosity and a sense of esoteric charm; they may function as rhetorical devices to engage readers, but do so knowingly and with purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentation about speed of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: He could taste no Praise till he had acquainted you in how short Space of Time he had deserved it; and was not so much led to an Ostentation of his Art, as of his Dispatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not boast about how quickly a piece was produced; such claims are a form of false wit and diminish artistic seriousness. Pride in rapid output is an anti-pattern to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject mechanical or formulaic methods for making verse
rubrics_metrics.description: This Virtuoso... contrived Tables by which any one without knowing a Word of Grammar or Sense... may... compose or rather to erect Latin Verses... a Mill to make Verses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ersatz, machine-like procedures (tables, combinatory devices, 'mills') that manufacture poetry without sense or feeling; these contrivances produce artificial, incoherent verse and are satirized as false wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer naturalness and avoid affected conceits in lyric poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: She followed Nature in all her Thoughts, without descending to those little Points, Conceits, and Turns of Wit with which many of our modern Lyricks are so miserably infected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In lyrical writing favor sincere, natural expression of passion and image over petty cleverness, forced conceits, or mechanical wit; aim for genuine feeling rather than ornament for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve image, sentiment, ease, and spirit in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Translation has preserved every Image and Sentiment of Sappho, notwithstanding it has all the Ease and Spirit of an Original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In translating poetry, seek fidelity to the original's images and sentiments while rendering the work in natural, spirited language in the target tongue; balance literal fidelity with readability and poetic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor pathetic simplicity in translating certain odes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Reader will find in it that Pathetick Simplicity which is so peculiar to him, and so suitable to the Ode he has here Translated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For certain lyric originals (e.g., Sappho), preserve the simple, pathetic tone—avoid over-elaboration or foreign ornamentation that would obscure the original's emotional clarity.
